speechtext:
I have the honour to inform the house that the Clerk has laid upon the table the 19th report of the clerk of petitions: Nineteenth Report of the Clerk of Petitions
Friday, March 4, 1960
The clerk of petitions has the honour to report that he has examined the petition of Carl Hamilton of the city of Ottawa, presented on March 3 by Mr. Howard, and finds that it is not in the form required by the standing orders and practice of this house since the signature of the petitioner does not appear on the same page as the prayer. For that reason the clerk of petitions has the honour to submit that the said petition should not be received.
Respectfully submitted,
Clerk of Petitions
In accordance with the rules of the house, if it is reported that a petition does not comply with the rules it cannot be received.

subtopic: PETITION WITH RESPECT TO APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I be heard on that point? I assume that the standing order referred to is subsection 6 of standing order 70, which reads as follows:
Petitions may be either written or printed; provided always that when there are three or more petitioners the signatures of at least three petitioners shall be subscribed on the sheet containing the prayer of the petition.
This is the only reference I can find in the standing orders to signatures of the petitioners. You will note that it refers to when there are three or more, and makes no reference to there being one or two petitioners. In this regard I should like to point out how this provision arose. I refer to Bourinot's "Parliamentary Procedure and Practice", the edition of 1884, which makes reference on page 263 to irregularities in petitions, the number of petitioners and so on. It says:
A large number of petitions are not received every session on various grounds of irregularity. The house will refuse to receive a memorial containing no prayer.
This is the relevant part.
Every petition should have the signatures of "at least three petitioners on the sheet containing the prayer."
I would then refer to footnote No. 2, which reads as follows:
The reason of this rule may be understood by reference to a statement of Lord Clarendon (Hist, of Rebellion, II, 357) that, in 1640, "when a multitude of hands was procured, the petition itself was cut off, and a new one framed suitable to the designing hand, and annexed to the long list of names which were subscribed to the former. By this means many men found their hands subscribed to petitions of which before they had never heard."
The reason for the standing order, which makes reference to three or more petitioners having their names on the same page as the prayer, was to overcome the practice of petitioners signing their names to something to which they subscribed and their names then being cut off and attached to another petition which was presented to the house. The purpose was to ensure that when there were three or more petitioners, three of the names had to be subscribed to the same sheet as the prayer to indicate that at least some of the many petitioners had subscribed to the petition itself, and so that their signatures would not be attached to a petition without their knowledge.
I think you will find that is the reason behind subsection 6 of standing order 70 in the standing orders today, and why it only makes reference to when there are three or more petitioners and no reference to when there are only one or two.
That being the case, I think it should be found that this petition meets the provisions of the standing order in all respects and should be received and proceeded with.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PETITION WITH RESPECT TO APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext:
I am not sure that I have any authority to consider the acceptance of a petition that has been reported on unfavourably by the clerk of petitions, whose duty it is to certify to the house whether or not the petition complies with its requirements. But in any case I have anticipated that the apparently rather technical objection might be disputed, and I should like to say that in my view the argument the hon. member has just made is not substantiated by the practice in the past.
The rule has been interpreted as though it meant that the sheet containing the prayer must have at least three signatures. Unfortunately the rule is not drawn as clearly as it might be. The rule in the other place is clear because it indicates that is the practice. But our practice has always been

Proposed Legislation
to read the rule as though it meant that where there is more than one signature, at least three of them must be on the page containing the prayer. It is a salutary rule. As all hon. members who have had experience with petitions will appreciate, it is easy enough to sign a sheet with other names on it and not have much knowledge of what the prayer of the petition is.
In support of my view I would cite Bourinot's fourth edition at pages 233 and 234 and at page 235, where Bourinot states as follows:
And the petition should then close with the formal words; "And your petitioners as in duty bound will ever pray." Here follow the signatures of the petitioners which must be in writing and at least three signatures, if there are so many, must he on the same sheet with the prayer of the petition.
On January 31, 1913 Mr. Speaker Sproule ruled a petition out of order because there were not three names on the sheet containing the prayer. That is found in the Journals of the House of Commons, 1912-13 at page 210.
Bourinot at page 263 of the first edition states as follows with regard to that rule, now standing order 70, subsection 6 to which the hon. member referred:
But this rule is never interpreted as precluding a single petitioner from approaching the house; it simply refers to petitions signed by a number of individuals.
The matter is not one difficult of correction, but I think the better course is to reject the petition at this stage.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: 619. Acquisition of the pipe lines (including the oil therein) and related facilities that are located in Canada and that belong to the United States government and form part of what is known as the Canol pipe line system, $670,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when we rose at 10 o'clock last night we were dealing with this item concerning the purchase by the Canadian government of this section of the Canol pipe line. I have taken the opportunity of doing a little bit of study on this matter. I can assure the committee it is only a little bit, and I have only scratched the surface. However, I have at least ascertained enough to realize that this is a good bargain. I see, according to one report, that the roads that were opened up in this area of the country in connection with this pipe line amounted to more than the Alaska highway. Included along with that there are a number of airfields which possibly could be of great use in that part of the country.
I am not concerned at all about what kind of a bargain Canada is getting. However, I am a bit concerned with just what Canada is going to do with this bargain when she gets it. I was wondering if the minister could inform the house as to just what the future disposition of this pipe line will be.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I told the committee last night that the disposition was now before the government. The first objective is to obtain this pipe line in the right of Canada; then we have the choice of selling or leasing.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before the item carries there is a point or two I wish to make concerning the remarks I made last night. I am afraid they were very poorly put because of the construction that may be placed upon them. I should like to clarify these remarks by saying that the existence of competition in the Yukon in the matter of the supply and distribution of petroleum products is a very welcome thing as long as that competition brings about a reduction in the cost of petroleum products to Yukon users.
I said last night there may be some people who are doubtful that the operation of additional lines of supply into the Yukon will indeed have the effect of lowering the prices of petroleum products throughout the Yukon, which are extremely high now. At the moment Yukon Petroleum Distributors, who are an arm of the White Pass and Yukon Route,
Supply-Northern Affairs have as their competitors Alaska-Yukon Refiners and Distributors, Limited, Alaska-Yukon Pipe Lines Limited and Yukon Shamrock Petroleum Distributors, Limited; these are the main suppliers of petroleum products.
The fear I have is that by some disposition of the pipe line that is being taken over by the Canadian government the cost of petroleum products in the Yukon will rise rather than be lowered. Any competition, of course, that will result in the lowering of the cost of petroleum products to Yukon users is very welcome indeed. I would like to put this question to the minister, and it is a very important one in so far as we in the Yukon are concerned. What guarantees can the minister give the committee now that the cost of petroleum products will either remain the same or be lower because of the Canadian government's acquisition of this pipe line facility and whatever they propose doing with it in the future? What security has the minister to offer the people of the Yukon that the status quo in so far as the cost of petroleum products is concerned will be maintained by this government action?
I have one further allusion to make before I take my seat, Mr. Chairman. We in the Yukon have been crucified in the past, particularly under the Liberal administration, by this business of government competing with private enterprise. In almost every phase of industry, little as it may be in the Yukon, the government has entered into direct competition with local industry. This I hope is not the intention here, as was suggested by the hon. member for Kootenay West yesterday.
In past years the government have competed through the army, through the air force, through Canadian National Telegraphs, through almost every arm of government under the Liberal administration. This, I am very happy to say, has almost tapered off, but naturally at the moment I for one would be loath to see any reinstitution of this invidious process come about.
I would appreciate it if the minister would not mind answering that one rather important question for me in regard to the assurance that he has to give now to the committee as to the security which the people of the Yukon may expect in regard to the maintenance of present price levels of petroleum products in the Yukon and, in the alternative, the assurance that they might expect that prices will in no way rise as a result of the action the government is contemplating here.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in my report to the committee last night I indicated that one of the ways in which we could protect the public interest in relation

Supply-Northern Affairs to the sale of petroleum products in the Yukon in connection with the Canol pipe line was by insisting that whatever arrangement is made, the provision of being a common carrier would be enforced. As I understand it, if we set up this requirement that the pipe line be operated as a common carrier, then we have the right to ask that the company file its tariff with the responsible or appropriate government agency, and also that it must submit its financial and statistical reports to the same appropriate government agency and also submit to the usual justification, or to the usual control, under the jurisdiction of the appropriate government agency.
I cannot speak of those things with too much precision because they are the matters which are now under consideration by the government; but I would suggest to the hon. member for Yukon that this would be the best way of guaranteeing that there was a minimum cost applied to the oil moving through those lines.
Second, there is another protective device that we could put into effect, namely to apply the rules that apply to pipe lines in other parts of the country; to see that their returns on capital expenditure and maintenance operation costs are not more than those allowed to a similar type of industry in the rest of Canada. I believe this is all I can say at this time, Mr. Chairman, as to the protective devices that we are considering to make certain that the price of petroleum fuel in the Yukon is kept to a minimum.
The hon. member for Yukon emphasized the advantage there is in maintaining price competition. In view of the energy and aggressiveness of the oil and gas industry I think this competition will bring reduced prices to the consumers of petroleum products in the Yukon.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in discussing this particular situation with the hon. member for the Yukon I discovered, much to my surprise, that the price of gasoline is even higher there than it is in my own area, which I thought was as high as the price in any place in Canada. I understand that gasoline there is as high as 57 cents a gallon as against 54 cents in my area. I find this difficult to understand. I find it difficult to understand why gasoline practically at the very source should have this high price. It makes one wonder just how much benefit the people in that part of the country have received from competition there. I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the record of the oil companies across the country has not tended to show that there


is in fact any competition among them, but rather that they prefer to fix prices and all that sort of thing.
The hon. member for Yukon has expressed the desire that the benefits of competition to the consumer should apply up there. I would say, Mr. Chairman, this is a commendable objective; but I find it difficult to follow his reasoning when he is so against the idea of a crown corporation, or any government body, entering this competitive field with a view to benefiting the consumer. Fears were expressed yesterday by both the hon. member for Yukon and the hon. member for Vancouver South. They both seemed to have a terrible fear about a crown corporation being formed to operate this resource that the Canadian government and taxpayers are purchasing.
I would say that I entertain different fears altogether. I am much more afraid of the Canadian taxpayers being used again as they have been used in the past and not getting any benefit from competition; because oil companies, as has often occurred in the past, tend to fix their prices rather than compete with one another. But in addition the taxpayers may be stuck with the purchase price of a line that may be turned over to private industry, which will receive the benefits at the expense of the public. I suggest that both the minister and the government take special care in this case to ensure that this does not happen, as it has happened in the past.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before the minister replies may I explain, with great respect, to the hon. member for Timmins, who obviously is unfamiliar with the facts as they exist, that contrary to his expectations the formation of a crown corporation to handle any of the petroleum distribution function now carried on by these two competitors in the Yukon would have very serious effects on the economy of the Yukon. One of the present suppliers is the White Pass and Yukon, who as their petroleum distribution arm operate Yukon Petroleum Distributors.
The White Pass and Yukon route has been one of the most substantial contributors to the development of the Yukon territory for the past 60 years. They have a shipping operation at the coast. They have a railroad operation of 106.5 miles from Skagway in the Alaskan panhandle to Whitehorse. They have a trucking operation along the Alaska highway. All these operations are interdependent upon each other, including their petroleum distribution operation. If you detract from the petroleum distribution operation then you detract from the whole

operation and there can be only one result. Fuel and all other consumer products will cost the people of the Yukon more, building costs will go up, and economic development will be retarded. Therefore any interference by a crown corporation operating a petroleum distribution system in the Yukon is just untenable. No matter how attractive it may appear to the hon. member for Timmins as a socialistic proposal, it would simply result in pulling the rug right out from underneath the main transportation operation in the whole of the Yukon territory.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am rather afraid that the hon. member for Yukon is confusing the issue. A crown corporation may appear to be untenable to him, but he is certainly confusing the issue. I understood the minister to say that because of the arrangement between the sovereign governments of the United States and Canada no private company can take over the segment of the pipe line. It must be done by the government of Canada, and the purpose of the estimate now before us is to take over, on the basis of the understanding between the two governments, a certain pipe line operation in Canada. In that respect I have no objection and do not question it at all.
But is Canada going to take over this operation and then let it die? The answer must be no, because we are going to spend somewhere in the neighbourhood of $700,000 in order to take it over. But we are not going to spend $700,000 to take over this segment of the pipe line and then discard it. It is going to be used. How is it going to be used? It is not a question of entering into competition and wiping out a company which for many years has operated railroad and other transportation facilities. According to the minister, this line will be operated on the principle of a common carrier. If so it is required; because if it is not required then Canada has no business spending $700,000 to purchase something which is going to be discarded. It must be required for the economy of the Yukon. If it is, then on what basis of misunderstanding can it be said that Canada, which is putting up the capital to purchase this segment, should not operate it as a common carrier?
If the government is not going to operate it through a crown company as a common carrier, then it is going to lease it to others who will use it as a common carrier. Surely if that is the viewpoint of the minister the line will not be entering into competition with whatever else there is in the Yukon. The government must feel that it is necessary and essential, and for the life of me I cannot
Supply-Northern Affairs understand why the government should spend $700,000 of the people's money to acquire a segment of a common carrier and then not operate it.
To deal specifically with what the hon. member for Yukon has said, if the line is going to be used by private enterprise then what the government is doing is relieving private enterprise from making the required expenditure by having the taxpayers put up the necessary capital. That takes my mind back to a few years ago in the house when the Liberals put up the capital for a pipe line in northern Ontario. Why should the people of Canada provide capital for private enterprise? If it will pay private enterprise to operate this common carrier which is now going to be bought by the government, then why should it not be possible for the government to maintain ownership and operate it with a view to earning a return on the taxpayers' money in the interests of the people of Canada who are making the capital investment?
I am afraid the hon. member for Yukon is trying to argue both ends against the middle. His interest is that private enterprise should not have to put up the capital expenditure but should reap the benefit from expenditure of the taxpayers' money, whereas we in this party say that if the taxpayers put up the money the government should operate the line for the benefit of those who have put up the money. How anyone can have an argument against that I do not know.
There is no argument against the principle of crown corporations, because the present and past governments have operated a number of crown corporations. I cannot conceive of even the Conservative members of this house-at least I hope I cannot-suggesting that we now get rid of our crown corporations in the interests of Canada because they may be in competition with private enterprise or because, although Canada puts up the money, private enterprise gets the benefit. If that argument is correct then out goes the C.B.C., out goes T.C.A., out goes Polymer-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Out goes the C.C.F.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
No, sir, that would really have the C.C.F. in; because whether or not my friend likes the term, and it is not one that I like either, one sees continual references in the newspapers to the term "creeping socialism". The developments in private enterprise are making governments accept, year after year, the policies of public ownership, crown corporations. However, that is getting into a discussion of fundamental policies, and I want to come back to this subject which is before us.

Supply-Northern Affairs
If the development of the economy of the Yukon territory does not require this line, then the government has no business spending $700,000 to acquire it. This is the taxpayers' money. If the economy of the Yukon can use this pipe line, then the expenditure of $700,000 of the taxpayers' money by this government should be protected. If it is going to make money for private enterprise, and they want to use it, then it is the responsibility of the government using the taxpayers' money to operate the pipe line as a common carrier so the profit return will come to the people whose money is invested in the line. We are asked this afternoon to approve an item of $700,000.
Now I ask you, just how can you answer that point unless it is the view of the minister and the government, as well as that of the hon. member for Yukon, that the taxpayers of Canada shall make a capital investment for the profit return of private enterprise. Well, that may be the view of the hon. member for the Yukon and the government, but it is not ours. We are now saying to the minister that if the acquisition of this segment of the pipe line is required in the interests of Canada and the Yukon, we are going to vote for this expenditure; but we are asking that the pipe line be retained for the benefit of the economy of Canada. We should make the capital expenditure for the profit of the people of Canada, and not as a subterfuge to assist private enterprise in making a quicker profit as a result of the investment of the taxpayers' money.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I wonder if I might ask a few short, simple questions of the minister which might clarify this matter in the minds of the rest of us who are not engaged in, shall I call it, the private war between the hon. member for Vancouver East and the hon. member for Yukon. As I understand it there was an appraisal made of this pipe line, that is the present day value of it, and that figure was given by the minister. I believe it was some $1.7 million. The purchase price, I believe, was set at $585,000 for the pipe line, and the balance of the price is made up for oil presently in the line and storage facilities. Am I correct in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes. The only correction would be that the $585,000 was for the pipe line and appurtenances, things connected with the pipe line, and the balance is made up of the cost of the oil in the line. There was one other factor which I could look up in a few minutes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
What I am getting at is the price to be paid for the line which is under discussion, as set against the appraisal, and

that is $585,000 against the figure of $1.7 million. I think that is correct, and the figures were given last night.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I should like to correct those figures. The figure I quoted last night is the estimated current commercial value, $1.7 million, and that is correct. Then it was agreed by the United States and Canada, as a result of the meeting of September 9, 1959, that the transfer price should be $617,000, roughly. I used the figure of $585,000, which is incorrect; it should be $617,000. In addition to the transfer price it was also agreed we would take over the oil in the three-inch line, plus a reasonable charge for handling, and the value of this oil was calculated to be $51,000. Now, if you add the $51,000 and the $617,000, as well as some small extra amounts, you get the figure in the estimate of $670,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I have just one or two further questions. I understand that the government was obligated by notes in existence between the two countries to take over this asset when it was no longer used for the purposes for which it was originally constructed. It is no longer used for those purposes because the United States government has put in a facility of its own to service the military and other requirements in Alaska; is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I tried to
make this very clear last night, Mr. Chairman, when I said, in answer to a question by the hon. member for Kootenay West, that the line was built in 1942. As part of the agreement by which these lines were constructed, Canada agreed to purchase these facilities when the war ended. Negotiations have been carried on since that time and they were completed last September, in 1959. In so far as the military part of it is concerned, the United States has different methods of getting its fuel into Alaska, and I believe I would be fair in saying it is hoped that the three-inch pipe line that runs from Haines Junction up to Fairbanks might also be used to bring additional supplies for United States use in that area.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
May I ask the minister two
questions. He is recommending, in accordance with an agreement with the United States and also because he feels the acquisition is in the interests of the economy of that part of Canada, the expenditure of this money in order to acquire the pipe line. If that is correct, and I presume it is or he would not be asking parliament to authorize the expenditure of this money, does he not then agree that if it is a good deal and necessary to assist the economy in this part of

Canada, since the taxpayers' money is being used the line should be operated by the government of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
It is probably
a weakness of mine that I do not like to overexaggerate the importance of these things.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Will the minister say that about his speech over the radio two weeks ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Always.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
It was the most
exaggerated speech I ever heard.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Don't you read
your own?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: This pipe line, which was constructed during the war, cost a tremendous amount of money. It was built for reasons other than those which we are discussing now. It was for military reasons.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
You are now asking us to
authorize this purchase, not for military reasons but for the economy of that part of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Nothing could
have been more fortunate for this new territory which has been sitting there pretty well idle for 50 or 60 years awaiting a reconstruction period.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: This is the usual modesty.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
This new young community of Whitehorse in the southern part of Yukon will take to this pipe line as a person who is drowning takes to a lifesaver, because without this fuel coming in from seaboard sources and with the limited population there is in the Whitehorse area, which is mainly a transportation centre, it would be severely limited if it did not have access to this oil. If oil had to be brought in from Alaska or from Peace river, a long way from the source, the cost would be much higher than it is today.
The economics of this area at the moment are doubtful enough without taking away this pipe line from them. First of all, the pipe line is a very valuable physical asset. At the moment it is being used to bring oil into the territory because at the present time oil is not available in the territory. We hope that at some time in the future economic activities in the area will expand and create greater uses for this pipe line. This brings us to the question the hon. member raised about what we should do with it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
If the government are buying it, why do they not operate it if it has that value?
Supply-Northern Affairs

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Obviously under the agreement we had to buy it. It was part of an international understanding. Now that we have bought it and own it, or rather we have not got it until we pass this estimate but when we do have it we will have this facility in the right of the crown of Canada. We have several alternatives. One is to sell it to one or two companies that now operate in the area. The other is to lease it; and of course the alternative, if we favour going into the business, is for the government to run it through a crown corporation.
I am going to suggest that with this very reduced price of roughly $700,000, while we will have an asset that at the present time, because of the smallness of the population of Yukon, is not worth too much as far as returns are concerned, to have this asset when the population grows and the demand grows will be a great advantage to the people of Canada.
One of the points being considered in the argument as to whether we should sell it outright or keep it as a government property is this expectation of an increased population later on. If we were to sell it, we would have to sell it at a price which would give the company that operated it a reasonable return over the next few years of expectation in this part of the territory. If we were to hold it and lease it, then we would obviously lease it at a return that would give us not only some control over the price of the product to the consumer but some opportunity of getting out of it the money that the taxpayers put into it.
I would therefore suggest to the hon. member that one of the strong arguments for leasing is that you have the right to renew the lease. You have the right to renew the terms. On the one hand you have to consider the consumers of petroleum products in the Yukon, and on the other hand you have to consider the taxpayer getting his investment back. If this territory grows and expands; if in future this area blossoms as we hope it will, this asset of ours may become a very sizeable asset; and if we were to sell it at this time it might prove, four or five years from now, to have been a serious mistake.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: You are not going to sell?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I simply state that the matter is now under the consideration of the government. I gave the arguments which are being used back and forth as to the pros and cons of selling versus leasing.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
That is the very point. As a matter of fact it is rather unfair of the minister that he will not tell us. He has
1742	HOUSE OF
Supply-Northern Affairs given the arguments against selling. We are being asked to authorize this expenditure but we are not told whether it is to be sold or, if it comes to a lease, whether it is going to be short term or long term and whether the taxpayers of this country are going to be completely protected, especially on the lease.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Is it not a fact that the rates for the throughput of this pipe line are fixed by the national energy board, and that one of the criteria used is the rent paid or the capital invested, as the case may be, by the applicant to obtain the pipe line? So whether it is rented or sold, in any event the capital charge, whether by way of rent or purchase price, is a direct factor in the cost and the protection of the consumer in the Yukon lies in the fixing of the rates for transmission of the product by that board.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes, that is right. As I said earlier, all these matters of tariffs and financial returns come before the appropriate government agency, and I was careful in what I said as to which agency it was.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I recognize the hon. member for Yukon.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Chairman, for seeing me finally. With great respect to the hon. member for Vancouver East I cannot allow some of the wild statements he made a few moments ago to go unchallenged. Rather than my being confused, as he alleged, I think it is more a case of the shoe being on the other foot.
I am sure the hon. member now realizes, since he has been asking these questions of the minister relating to the requirement of the international agreement between Canada and the United States, that it is a commitment of the government that the pipe line must be taken over as a condition of that international agreement. You must either abide by this agreement or you must abrogate it. I am sure the hon. member for Vancouver East would be the last person to suggest that the government should abrogate its commitments internationally, and this is one of them; namely that they must take over and purchase the pipe line. This estimate is for that purpose. At least that is my understanding of the way the minister has explained the matter.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am not quarrelling about that matter. What are we going to do with it after we get it?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The hon. member for Vancouver East made several statements about


the reason for the pipe line being taken over and why are we spending this money on it. I am just pointing out to him that my understanding of the minister's explanation is that we must do it because it is a term of an international agreement. This fact surely should be clear now to the hon. member.
As the hon. member for Vancouver East points out, the fact that the pipe line is going to be used as a common carrier does not detract one iota from the facility of that common carrier being used in a competitive fashion, because one distributor can compete with another distributor through the same common carrier, surely. At the moment the line from Skagway to Whitehorse, a distance of 106.5 miles, is available. I understand it is still being used by only one distributor, but it has been declared a common carrier and it may be so used. Any other distributor can come in there and carry his product over that same line and compete. The capacity of that line from Skagway to Whitehorse is 45 million imperial gallons per year. The total consumption of Yukon last year was roughly 15 million gallons. Hence there is plenty of capacity in the one line.
There is another thing upon which the hon, member for Vancouver East did not comment when he was picking holes in my submissions a moment or two ago, namely the historical contribution which the White Pass and Yukon Railway has made to the development of Yukon and which it will continue to make. This company is a pioneer in transportation, and its function is still necessary to our development there. By instituting any crown corporation it would have the effect of diluting the effectiveness of the White Pass and Yukon Railway as a transportation organization of Yukon, and would have only one result, namely that of retarding development in that area.
Make no mistake. My views as to competition are shortly, clearly and concisely put when I say that competition is a very necessary element in any economy. If we had competition with this transport organization up there it would result in a lowering of the prices in the Yukon of all consumer items. That is a very desirable thing, and if we can gain this competition by building new roads, new railroads or new pipe lines, then let us do it as long as the end result will be a reduction in the cost to the people of the Yukon of the goods they purchase from these various organizations.
There is one other point I want to make, and that is that we in the Yukon, at any rate, have had just about a bellyful of government coming along and competing with local industry. The R.C.A.F. build their own

garages; the Canadian National Telegraphs build their own houses; the army build their own structures, and the territorial government have their own development program. All of this has tapered off to the point where it is almost non-existent today, but that is what used to exist up there. Because of this we could not build up any local industry. We could not build it up to the point where it is now, after two years, where we can tackle multimillion dollar road jobs, and so on; industries which are essential to the development of the north. I can only suggest again that if a crown organization is organized to take over the petroleum distribution system, local industry will once again be stifled.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the minister has told us that this is a very valuable physical asset worth at the present time about nearly three times what we are paying for it. He has also told us that it provides an essential service which will make the line more valuable as the population of the Yukon goes up.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: After I have finished. I have not said enough yet to warrant asking a question.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: If the hon. member would permit a question it might possibly affect what he is going to say. It will not take a second. Does the hon. member accept what I understood the minister to say, that what is being done is to carry out a binding agreement in writing?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is not a question. If you had waited until I finished you would not have asked that question. What I want to ask the minister is this.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: All this talk is unnecessary.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
It is not unnecessary. What I want to ask the minister is this. Can the minister give the house an assurance that this asset which the people are now acquiring will not be disposed of to any private party at any time for less than the fully appraised value at the time of sale?
I think that is what most of us on this side of the house are worried about. We have in mind what happened in the case of land belonging to the Indians which was sold for a song to a private individual, who later disposed of it for many times what he paid for it and made a huge capital gain. We on this side of the house certainly have a
Supply-Northern Affairs duty to get from the minister and the government an assurance that such a thing will never be permitted in the case of this pipe line.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is very true that we have to keep faith with the United States according to the agreement we signed some 18 years ago, but it is equally true that we must keep faith too with the Canadian taxpayer with regard to this matter That is our only concern.
Again, Mr. Chairman, I fail to follow the reasoning of the hon. member for the Yukon, who said that if this line remained under public ownership it would stifle the whole country; that competition from public ownership will stifle everything, whereas competition from private enterprise will not. I fail to follow his reasoning through. In fact you could almost draw from his remarks, Mr. Chairman, the inference that the concern is more for the business there than it is for the public, the taxpayers as a whole.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is not true.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I would like to point out just one instance where a crown corporation has worked to the benefit of the public at large. All you have to do is refer to insurance companies in Saskatchewan. Insurance companies across the country have special rates for the province of Saskatchewan because they have to compete with a crown corporation there, and it is of benefit to the public and the taxpayers that that is so. I say the same thing could result elsewhere.
There is one other question I would like to ask the minister. I understand from what little study I have been able to give to this matter that in addition to this pipe line, and in conjunction with it, there are these roads and also airports. What is to be the disposition of this sort of added facility? Are they going to become part and parcel of the whole thing, or will they remain under government control if the pipe line itself is leased or even is in danger of being sold?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, two matters have been talked about. The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo asked for an assurance from me. I have told the house very frankly about the arguments relating to sale versus lease. I think that should indicate how much we are aware of the fact that we have to protect both the consumer and the taxpayer. I am sure there will be no fire sale; we will take our time to make a good deal.
The hon. member for Timmins raised the question of the airfields and roads. I would suggest to him that most of the roads and airfields have disappeared in the course of

Supply-Northern Affairs time. Even though we have resurrected part of one of these roads, part of the highway up to Ross river, a little over 100 miles, the roads have disappeared. The culverts have all broken down and in many cases disappeared through the ravages of winter snow, the run-off, and so on. So I do not think there is any problem there. As to the other things we took over, I used the word "appurtenances" and I meant pumping stations and so forth, which are all part of the deal covered by the $670,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: May I ask one question for clarification. The minister said "the other things" after speaking about roads which have been taken over. As I understand it the United States never owned the roads and never claimed to own them. They were always roads which were owned by the government of Canada, and what we are buying under this item is the pipe line and the immediate facilities, such things as the pumping stations and, I assume, the other things which usually go with a pipe line; but certainly not the roads.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: There is no question of buying the roads.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to refer to the matters raised by this item now before us. The hon. member for Yukon mentioned last night the importance of this pipe line to an oil refinery, and I believe the minister also referred to that. Then the hon. member, as reported on page 1724 of Hansard, asked the minister:
Is the government in the course of negotiating with these people now for such a transfer ... ?
The minister replied on the same page:
-and the refining company has asked that they may take over the line that runs up to the Alaska border.
Then later on, as reported on page 1726, I asked the minister whether there were already agreements in existence and if there were what the terms of the agreements were, and the minister replied that there was no agreement. Well, I can understand that there cannot be an agreement until the government is actually the owner; it can hardly be expected to have an agreement until then. However, the minister in reply to the hon. member for Yukon indicated very clearly that negotiations are under way.
I should like to ask the minister whether he does not feel under an obligation to let us know the basis of these agreements which are now being negotiated. After all, if we are being asked to vote the money to buy the pipe line are we not entitled to know what the intentions of the government are?

I get the impression now that the government has not yet made up its mind whether it intends to lease the pipe line or dispose of it outright. Yet the minister admits that negotiations are actually under way.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Last night the hon. member asked if there were any agreements signed, and I said no. I also said last night in answer to a question that the Alas-ka-Yukon Refining Company had made an application to us to take over one of these pipe lines. The other thing I said which was significant was that this matter is now before the cabinet for a decision. In reaching this decision we have, naturally, to examine details of the operation of the pipe lines and the companies themselves in order to see how the public interest, the interest of the taxpayers, can be protected. While these negotiations are going on the hon. member has a perfect right to know what is decided, but I do not think he has a right to ask me to disclose the details, because the government has not decided on those details and until it has there is nothing I can tell the hon. member.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Could the minister indicate whether the application is to lease or to buy? The hon. gentleman has indicated that an application has been made to the government, to which the government is giving some consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Speaking from memory I believe it is an application to lease.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: There is just one question I want to ask the minister, and it is on an entirely different subject. In view of these vast oil developments we were told about on television last night, how soon does the hon. gentleman expect that oil produced in the north will be flowing through this pipe line?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The answer to the hon. member is, a lot sooner than he would be happy to know.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I should be happy to know that it was going to be tomorrow. But could the minister, out of his vast knowledge of the subject, hazard a guess as to whether it might be in 1961 or 1962?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate shows his vast ignorance of the subject when he suggests that oil or gas will flow out of the Yukon in 1960 or 1961. In my estimation the delineation of that field will run for five, six or seven years. The obtaining of markets will go simultaneously. I suggest to the hon. member, not to his discomfort, I hope, that he will be as

proud as I am as a Canadian if before 1965 we see energy fuels coming out of this region.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I suggest to the minister that he should tell some of these things to the Prime Minister, in order that the right hon. gentleman could give a more realistic picture to the Canadian public.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: May I say one thing here, and I mean it so sincerely-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Oh.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I have to say that because of the caterwauling and noise on the government side. I regret very much to have heard the minister of northern affairs say what he did, and I made just one comment on what has been said by the minister in answer to a question by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. When will the minister and his colleagues realize that in this committee we are all members of the House of Commons, and that irrespective of party we have love and patriotism for this country. It ill becomes the minister or anyone else, no matter where he sits, to state that any hon. member or any party in this house would not be happy to hear about developments in Canada. The sooner that sort of rot ceases the better it is going to be for us in this chamber and for the people of Canada.
We all love our country, and we all want to see it develop. It is bad for the minister to stand up and say that the official opposition or any private member would be unhappy to see development taking place. Surely the time for that kind of politics in Canada has long gone by.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I wonder if the minister could tell us what the approximate cost of the annual maintenance charges of this line amounts to?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I do not think I could give the hon. member that information.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The position, in a word, is that we are being asked to vote this money to take over the pipe line before the government knows what it is going to do with the pipe line, or before any definite arrangements have been made.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman suggesting that we should not fulfil our international obligations?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

In the case of each of the facilities included in the list referred to in A, the Canadian government and the United States government will each appoint one qualified appraiser whose joint duty it will be to appraise such facility in order to determine the fair market value thereof at the time and place of appraisal. 620.	National aviation museum-Administration, operation and maintenance, $75,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Has the minister a statement to make on this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Last autumn the government agreed to establish a national aviation museum as the first step toward the eventual setting up of a museum of science of Canada. The decision to proceed in 1959 was based in part on the wish of the government to commemorate suitably the anniversary of power flight. However, the fitness of recognizing the substantial and unique contributions made by this country in the field of civil aviation has been before the government for some time.
The problem of working out the concept of a national aviation museum was given to an associate committee of the national research council under the chairmanship of General A. G. L. McNaughton, known as the associate committee on the national aviation museum. This committee raised funds from private sources to enable a practical start to be made pending the provision of funds through normal government channels. Under an interim acting curator Mr. M. G. Kuhring, made available to this committee by the national research council-that is pending the recruitment of permanent personnel by the civil service commission-excellent progress has been made with the preparation of displays and their installation in the museum's temporary home. The temporary home is located on the second floor of the new Department of Transport air terminal at Uplands. This should provide adequate accommodation for the next few years.
My department which will administer the museum initially through the historic sites division of the national parks branch has recently been authorized by the treasury board to spend the sum of $45,000 for the purpose of developing this museum and operating it for the balance of the fiscal year. The balance

of the vote, $30,000, is made up of rent for the new accommodation. We expect that the museum will be ready to open this summer and it will probably be the same time as the opening of the Uplands airport terminal.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I received a clipping from one of our newspapers containing a report by the Canadian Press which indicated that this museum would only have space for one aircraft, that is the replica of the Silver Dart. I should like to make a plea on behalf of the Avro Arrow, that graceful and manoeuvrable bird which was shot down by a single poisoned arrow. It would make a wonderful museum piece. Had it been allowed to fly with the engines designed for it, it would have captured the world's speed record for Canada. It would make a wonderful museum piece. Since it was cancelled the United States has changed its mind about interceptors. Now it would be delighted to have a plane as good as the Avro Arrow in the North American inventory and is asking Canada to equip its air defence squadrons with a lesser United States fighter. The Arrow would be a wonderful museum piece.

I understand that this item is to cover the expenses of the royal commission on coal, the appointment of which was announced by the Prime Minister on August 20 of last year. In making the announcement the Prime Minister said the government felt that the coal problem was a special one and so urgent as to require a special inquiry rather than be considered by the Borden commission on energy. I note in this press release, which was made at the time and which came from the Prime Minister's office, the Prime Minister pointed out that subsidies alone were not a final answer to the coal problem, and indicated that a thorough study of the long term market outlook was required. What was striking was that the Prime Minister said a readjustment of coal production had to be made in such a way that the industry would serve its future markets efficiently and economically. I feel that this particular statement of the Prime Minister should be considered very seriously by members from the coal production areas who criticized so openly the statements made by Mr. Louis St. Laurent previously to the 1957 election.
We are pleased to see that this commission has been appointed and we feel that it will offer more to the coal producing areas of the maritimes than did the Borden commission on energy which did not even hold meetings in the maritimes, notwithstanding the promise made in this house by the Prime Minister to the effect that following the adjournment of the Borden commission in Montreal it would have further sittings in the maritime provinces. The fact is that the two briefs which were presented to the Borden commission from the maritimes were heard in Montreal on July 16 and July 22 of 1958.
We also deplore the fact that it took the government 14 months after we introduced the motion in this house, which in fact was done on June 30, 1958, to bring to the attention of the government the critical situation in the coal industry, when we exposed the lack of government policy to take care of the situation. It was over 14 months after that the Prime Minister made the announcement of this commission and admitted the seriousness of the situation.
I do not want to elaborate on this subject, Mr. Chairman. I know we shall have further

Supply-Privy Council opportunities during the present session to discuss the serious coal problems of the maritime provinces; but I wish to say that we rejoice in the appointment of Mr. Hand to head this commission. In fact, as was said in the Ottawa Citizen of October 8, 1959, that one of the best minds in Canada was to be applied to the problems of Canada's coal industry, especially in Nova Scotia where the situation is grave. Indeed, Ivan C. Rand, as he now is, after 16 years of impressive service on the Supreme Court of Canada, will be tackling one of the most formidable tasks of his career. If he cannot produce a happy solution, it is unlikely that anyone else can.
The Rand commission, Mr. Chairman, is holding sittings in the maritime provinces at the present time and we feel sure that if there is a solution to be found to the coal industry, the present commissioner, Ivan C. Rand, is the right man to have as head of this commission.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the best way to answer the question is to read from the appointment as to the particular duties of this commission. These gentlemen have been appointed commissioners under part I of the Inquiries Act to inquire into and report upon the respective merits of the alternate routes which might be followed by the railway line to be built from northern Alberta into the southern portion of the district of Mackenzie, Northwest Territories, for the purpose of providing access to and contributing to the development of that portion of the territories tributary to Great Slave lake.
I am sure that the commissioners are following the terms of their appointment and will certainly consider that aspect of the question to which the hon. member for Vancouver East has just referred. His suggestion certainly appears reasonable.

I have raised the question for one reason only. I want to point out this fact. If you are elected as a member of parliament you are under pressure. If you are in the opposition you are under pressure. As an electrician may I say that I did not blow the fuses and cause the lights to go out. As a matter of fact, if I talk long enough you will see the light. I should like to say this, Mr. Chairman-
Louder.

If you want to hear my voice I will let you have it. To carry on with what I was going to say, there is no question whatsoever that when you are elected to parliament you are under pressure. Individual members are under pressure, parties are under pressure, the official opposition is under pressure and I feel certain that the government is under pressure. From what I have been able to read in the past few months the government is under pressure as to the route this railroad is to take. I have no hesitation whatsoever in standing in my place today and

expressing the hope that the decision, whatever it may be, will not be made on the basis of local pressure, area pressure, provincial pressure or any other pressure. I hope that any decision as to the extension of the railway system in Canada will be based wholly and solely on what is in the best interests of the development of Canada and our economy.

This remains to be seen. The
original purchase was obviously a good purchase because the government was able to get all its money back, and then some, when it disposed of the property as being unsuitable for the purposes which the government had in mind. I would point out that the original purchase was a property adjoining Canada House. In fact, it could even have been connected to Canada House in Trafalgar square by an overhead bridge. It would have been a matter of great convenience to have had as many government offices as possible practically under one roof. No doubt that was a consideration important in the minds of those who made the decision in the first place. Whether it will be as economical to divide the staff at Canada House and have half in the new Canada House and half in the discarded United States embassy in Gros-venor square remains to be seen. We will have to find out how much money will be required to remodel this former United States building.
We shall also have to find out by experience whether or not it is an advantage to have the second Canada House in what is now known as Little America, Grosvenor square,

which is going to be an increasingly busy part of London because the new United States embassy and its offices will be located in that square. Parking is not going to be quite as easy and simple as the minister has indicated in his remarks.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It will still be a lot better than around the Hampton property.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It ought to be better, but it is not going to be an easy situation in that respect. Grosvenor square is not traffic free by any means. However, the minister has said that the decision has been taken. A great deal of money, no doubt, will be required to remodel this building. The minister has said it is going to house all the Canadian offices which will not be in Canada House, Trafalgar square. I have been informed, perhaps my information is not accurate, that there will only be available for office accommodation in this new building some 60,000 to 65,000 square feet, whereas the joint staff, et cetera, requires over 80,000 square feet for its accommodation.
I should like to have the minister confirm, if he can, the statement he has just made that there will be ample accommodation in this building for all the Canadian offices which will not be at Trafalgar square. I understand also one of the disadvantages of this building, which may have been responsible in part for the United States government giving it up, is that it includes a great many flats and that some of the leases on these flats cannot be taken over. There will be tenants in the building after we take it over. It is said it is the intention of the Canadian government to accommodate Canadian government officials in some of these flats, something to which I do not necessarily take exception at all. It may be a very good thing to do. Presumably they will pay rent for their flats and it will be a convenience and help to have them accommodated on the property.
However, with accommodation of that kind in this building, and with the floor space as I have indicated, I do not see how all the Canadian government offices could be put in this one building. The minister has said that is going to be done, and perhaps the information I have is not accurate. I wish he would correct me if I am wrong in that regard. He may also tell us how much money will be required to remodel this building. I would have hoped that if we could not find suitable accommodation at Hampton, it could have been found in some place other than Grosvenor square. I understand there may have been accommodation in Berkeley square which is even

closer to Canada House. This accommodation might have been more suitable than any building in Grosvenor square. I bring this matter to the attention of the minister and perhaps it will serve to correct some of the exuberance and optimism which he has just exhibited.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am still exuberant. I should like to point out that in the original estimate of saving of $1,675,000, there has been included $250,000 as the cost of remodelling the offices and getting them in shape. The sum of $250,000, therefore, has already been added and we still have the saving of $1,675,000 to the Canadian taxpayer.
My understanding is, also, that not only have we enough space but at the moment we have too much space for all the other offices and that includes the department of defence which is going to move in there. It is true there are some tenants on the top floor, but we are having no trouble with their leases. As we wish them to move out, they will move out. We hope, in the meantime, to keep all the property we can vacant. We not only have enough property, but I ask my friend to recall this was a United States embassy for a country of 170 million, and we have acquired it for a country of 17 million. We have this property for a very reasonable price under all the circumstances and have lots of room, not only for our present requirements but for expansion as well.
In so far as the square footage is concerned, I could not give my friend an answer on that at the moment. I shall be glad to supply him with it when the figures are available. If there are any further questions, I would be delighted to try to answer them.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The fact that this building was once a United States embassy for a country of 175 million has nothing whatever to do with the question because this was only one United States building. They had half a dozen others scattered around London in which they housed members of the embassy staff and other United States government agencies.
However, the important thing is that the minister has said all the Canadian government offices that will not be accommodated in Trafalgar square Canada House can be accommodated in this building. He has given a specific assurance that that can be done. If that is the case, and I have been informed to the contrary, then of course that puts a different light on this transaction. It will be interesting to ask the minister a
Supply-Public Works
year from now how many Canadian officers are still accommodated outside the building in Grosvenor square.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I understand, in reply to the Leader of the Opposition, that the Leader of the Opposition himself was not in favour of carrying on with the Hampton site and realized the former government had made an error.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I do not think that is true. The minister said I was not in favour of carrying on that Hampton site. I do not know where he got evidence to that effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: You had a unified cabinet, I know, but the hon. member's individual opinion was against it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is a strange statement for the minister to make, and I do not know where he got evidence of that.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Perhaps you will verify it for me.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is an even stranger position for the minister to take. I subscribed to the decision to purchase the Hampton property. It seemed to be a good decision to make and, perhaps, it will turn out to be a better decision than the one the present government has made; that remains to be seen. The fact that it was good business to purchase this site was shown by the fact that the government could sell it at a profit. I have told the minister my information is that there are only 65,000 square feet in this building and that the staffs require 81,000 square feet. The minister has said there is going to be ample accommodation in this building for all Canadian offices not accommodated at Trafalgar square. We shall find out about that in the months to come.

I rise on a question of privilege Mr. Chairman. I think it is unfortunate that we are in darkness but that you as chairman should try to make it clear to the fourth estate that although the House of Commons is in darkness, the speeches are most enlightening.

May I ask the minister
whether plans have been prepared for the alteration of that building?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
I want to tell my hon. friend, and I should have added it, that we have today Mr. Freeze, the head of the property department who himself is an architect, over in England consulting on the matter. I should add this; my hon. friend, the Leader of the Opposition, speaks with a certain amount of finality on the question of whether the actual

Supply-Public Works
joint chiefs of staff aside from the department of defence and all its offices are staying behind. He states that is something about which there is some question and I am trying to put in a phone call at the present time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It is a good thing I did speak with some finality because the minister has just repudiated a statement he made a few moments ago in arguing how advantageous it was to buy this discarded United States embassy. A big advantage and one I must say appealed to me although it surprised me that all Canadian government offices not at Trafalgar House would now go into that building. But he has now said that the joint chiefs of staff, which is the Canadian organization in London outside of Canada House, may not go into it.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: We will check on that matter.
If I understood the minister correctly, he said the cost of alterations would be about $250,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: That is the estimate.
May I ask the minister how he can arrive at such a figure without having plans prepared?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: As I say, Mr. Chairman, the estimate of the cost of these changes is $250,000. All we can do is to accept the best estimate we can make at the time when the architect is over in England, if there is a variation in price, it will be brought to the attention of the house.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: May I ask the minister to confirm that in the earlier plans for the Hampton building all Canadian officers in London would have been accommodated in this adjunct to Canada House, including the joint staff?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I am glad my hon. friend raised that question. As a matter of fact, I am not particularly glad but it gives me an opportunity to point out that had the Hampton site been proceeded with and had the plans of the government of that day been consummated the whole department of defence in England-our representatives there-would have refused to go into the building and no plans were made for them to go there. I understand the matter came to cabinet and that it was approved that the department of defence should not be forced to go into this impossible site in the middle of one of the worst traffic arteries in the world.
I should like to ask a question in connection with the purchase. Is the property being acquired on the basis of freehold, copyhold or leasehold?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: May I just add one word more in answer to the Leader of the Opposition? My information is that the joint chiefs of staff as well as the other branches of the department of defence who are in London will be housed in the new Canadian building in Grosvenor square.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: We are back to the original statement that all Canadian government offices in London not at Trafalgar square will be in the new building. Is that the situation?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: That is our understanding. It will also interest my hon. friend to know that there are about 80,000 feet.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is that 80,000 feet in all or 80,000 feet in the building for offices alone?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Eighty thousand square feet of space in the building, which is 20 per cent more than the Liberal government planned to build on the Hampton site at a cost to Canada of $1,675,000 more than this Grosvenor square building.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That 80,000 square feet includes accommodation for several apartments, I believe. Does the minister deny that?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: My friend the Leader of the Opposition has been wrong in nearly every statement he has made.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister has contradicted himself already three times.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: After all, when he brings forward these strange things, I will send out and get information but it is hard to get a positive answer to a hypothetical question.
Can the minister not do what he recommended in another place during another session and have all the plans here before he attempts to put his estimates through?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: In answer to that question may I say that we have to get occupation of the property before we can do that?
May I point out that I was on my feet when the lights went out and that I was on my feet when the lights came on.
I should like an answer to my question. Are you acquiring freehold rights or leasehold rights to this property?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: We are getting, as I understand it, a 100-year, or almost that, leasehold which one gets in London in that area.
Is this to the property or to the actual building? I know that in London they are quite often separate. Is it all in one package? How far along in the 99-year term is this particular lease?

speechtext: We had to arrange with the borough, the council and after long deliberations succeeded in getting their consent to take over this long term lease.
