speechtext: 1. Departmental administration, including advisory committee on agricultural services, $777,657.

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in introducing the main estimates of the Department of Agriculture for the fiscal year 1960-61 I shall today, in view of the circumstances, merely review briefly some of the activities of the department and developments of interest during the past year.
The main estimates for the coming year at $113.5 million show an increase of $4.2 million over the amount provided in the main estimates and first supplementaries for the present year. There are minor increases and decreases in several items of expenditures, but additional requirements in connection with the South Saskatchewan river project represent the major portion of the net increase.
The amount provided for agriculture research is $30 million, which is about 27 per cent of the total departmental estimates. The production and marketing branch accounts for $54 million, about 50 per cent of the total. Under this provision comes the administration of a wide variety of agricultural legislation and policies, grants, subsidies, quality premium payments, freight assistance on western feed grains and the administration of the Agricultural Stabilization Act.
The third major category of departmental expenditure covers activities under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act, and the administrative costs of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. The provision for these is $26 million, about 23 per cent of the departmental total. The committee might be interested in developments with respect to some of the major P.F.R.A. activities.
Work on the South Saskatchewan project is proceeding on schedule. There was a delay last fall, due to weather conditions, in placing the fill for the embankments but it has been possible to catch up with this during the winter. Some 500 men have been working on the dam all winter.
The construction bridge will be completed by June. Contracts have been awarded to date to a total of some $16 million. It is expected that a further contract will be awarded shortly for the construction of the downstream half of the five diversion tunnels, which will bring the total to approximately $24 million.
Work is proceeding satisfactorily on the Watertown river diversion of the St. Mary river project, which is the remaining main works of that undertaking. Some 4,400 small water projects, consisting of dugouts and

Supply-Agriculture
small dams, were constructed during 1959. This represents a considerable increase over previous years.
Three new community pastures, totalling 156,000 acres, are being established in Manitoba. One, near McCreary, was completed in 1959 and will be in operation in 1960. Construction of two others in the Dauphin-Mossey River-Ethelbert area will be started this spring.
Operations under the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act are also proceeding satisfactorily. The main projects at present under way are the Tantramar and Annapolis river dams. The Tantramar dam, with the exception of some minor work to be done in the spring, is completed and is in operation. The Annapolis dam, which is a much larger project, is on schedule, and work on the main fill has begun. Closure of the dam is expected to take place in the fall of this year, leaving only a small amount of work to complete the project in 1961.
Under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act some 34,503 awards, to a total of approximately $11 million, have been made to date with respect to the 1959 crop. Because of the difficulties in completing harvest, it is not possible to make an accurate estimate of the total payments but they are expected to be in the order of $16 million. Payments for the 1958 crop total $23.1 million.
The health of animals division has continued to make good progress in brucellosis testing and in the establishment of brucellosis certified areas. This, of course, is extremely important in maintaining free access to the United States market for export cattle in view of the new regulations of the United States with respect to brucellosis certification. As members know, areas are accepted for brucellosis testing and certification on application from provincial governments. In the east, areas consist of counties; and in the west, municipalities or groups of municipalities. To the end of January, 378 areas with over 5 million head of cattle had been accepted for testing. Ninety areas, with 1.5 million head of cattle have been certified, and a further 124 areas are under test. To expedite the brucellosis testing, we have established new laboratories in Guelph, Winnipeg and Regina to supplement the facilities already provided in departmental laboratories at Vancouver, Lethbridge, Ste. Anne de Bellevue, Sackville, and at the main laboratory in Hull.
I think I will skip over a few other points I was going to make, particularly in connection with the grading of hogs, which we will go into when that particular item comes up.
[Mr. Harkness.l
Under the agricultural stabilization board support prices have been prescribed for 18 commodities during the past year. With respect to some of the commodities for which support prices have been prescribed, it has not been necessary for the board to enter into actual support operations, since the market prices have been above the support level. This is the case, for example, with cattle.
Of the 15 active programs, the market is supported in the case of five commodities by offers of outright purchase by the board. Eight commodities are supported by deficiency payments, now including eggs and hogs, and in two instances there are flat payments to producers.
Members who are familiar with the departmental organization will recall that last year we joined the previous experimental farm service and science service together into a research branch. In this we now have a cohesive organization in which the various scientific disciplines can be brought to bear under unified direction in dealing with specific research matters. The total organization includes, apart from Ottawa, 31 experimental farms, 17 substations, 29 laboratories and two forest nursery stations. In these, we are endeavouring to maintain a proper balance between fundamental and applied research and to make the best use of our scientific resources in the interests of Canadian agriculture. The more fundamental research is being conducted primarily at the more specialized research institutes and laboratories. The field establishments, as in the past, are continuing to concentrate on applied research problems of particular importance to their own areas.
A new forest biology laboratory was opened recently at Quebec city. Two other new major laboratories are now nearing completion on the experimental farm property at Fredericton and at Vancouver, on the campus of the University of British Columbia.
The committee will be interested to know that we are making progress in the establishment of animal research facilities on a property of more than 4,000 acres in the green belt southwest of Ottawa. The drawing up of plans has been under way for some time and we hope that construction on some of the functional buildings will start in the fall of 1960. Eventually all the livestock and poultry activities will be transferred from the central experimental farm to this new location, as will the main animal pathology laboratories of the health of animals division.
In these remarks I have dealt with some of the major highlights of departmental activities which I thought might be of interest to

the committee. I will, of course, be pleased to elaborate and provide any detailed information which may be desired during the consideration of individual items.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this afternoon I intend to say a few words generally with regard to the agricultural policy of this government, and then to deal with a request that was made by representatives of the western farmers in support of deficiency payments for wheat, oats and barley produced during the years 1955-56, 1956-57 and 195758. I will begin by simply outlining some of the general principles that this government has followed, particularly since I enunciated the general guiding principles that we intended to follow in a speech made in this house on August 30, 1958, as reported in Hansard of that day at page 4345.
In my speech on that occasion I dealt with the general plans of the government, with the viewpoint in general representative of the Conservative party policy. I set forth some of the stands that had been taken and were intended to be taken. Summarizing them, and without going into detail, they were, first:
The government proposes, subject to approval by parliament at the next session-
That was in 1959.
-to continue the fund to assist in the export of surplus wheat stocks to non-commercial markets under the Colombo plan.
I pointed out on that occasion that the amount contributed under the Colombo plan by Canada per year had been raised from some $34 million to $50, three years in advance. Second:
The government is studying in consultation with the provinces legislation to provide for a comprehensive crop insurance program.
On that occasion I said that it had been one of the demands of farmers in general throughout the years that something be done to protect, within reason, against the uncertainties to which agriculture is subjected. That portion of the policy, the long term policy for agriculture, has been carried into effect, as has the earlier one to which I referred. Third:
In recognition of the recurring hazard of drought to the stability of livestock production in the prairie provinces, the government has taken steps to provide assistance to provincial governments, which have the prime responsibility for meeting the needs of feed deficit areas, and is giving sympathetic study to the establishment, under provincial administration but with federal financial assistance, of a forage bank program.
This particular portion of the enunciated policy has not been carried out as yet. Fourth:
That the government is presently engaged in a comprehensive study and review of the Canadian
Supply-Agriculture
Farm Loan Act, the Farm Improvement Loans Act and the Veterans' Land Act, with a view to determining where enlargement of scope, expansion in function, or improvement in methods of operation may be required.
Also, increased credit through amendments to the Canadian Farm Loan Act and the authorized capital. Fifth:
As a means of meeting the small farm problem the government has under consideration ways and means of improving the level of living for farmers on small farms by means of better land use, encouraging the formation of economic family farm units, improving technical training-
And so forth. That particular portion is still under consideration.
Then plans are under way for a national conservation conference which will have important and far-reaching effects. I shall make reference to that in a moment.
Then I dealt with a request which had been made even at that time respecting deficiency payments and I stated:
The government has come to the conclusion that deficiency payments, however attractive they appear to be at first glance, would not provide a solution to the problems facing prairie agriculture but would indeed create new problems.
I set out the reasons for that view and I ended by saying:
For these general reasons we have come to the conclusion that deficiency payments to producers are not in the long run interest of either the western grain producer or the nation as a whole.
Then I referred later in my remarks to a request which had been made throughout the years by western farmers for the establishment of a two-price system for wheat, having in mind a domestic price considerably higher than the selling price of wheat for export. The proposal has to do, of course, with wheat for human consumption within Canada, the farm organizations having contended throughout the years that the Canadian consumer had been getting wheat too cheaply. As found at page 4347 I made this point in connection with the proposal:
An increase of 50 cents per bushel in the price of wheat for domestic consumption would be reflected in an increase of only 6.5 cents per bushel on the basis of total marketings.
On the basis of an average consumption of wheat within Canada through the years of 45 million bushels, an increase of 50 cents a bushel, as I said a moment ago, on wheat for domestic consumption over the world price would result in a sum of approximately $22J million. On that occasion I announced that, regard being had to these circumstances, a payment to western grain producers of $1 per acre up to a maximum of 200 acres per farm would be provided, or a total amount of some $40 million. As it turned out, the amount was somewhat in excess of that sum.

Supply-Agriculture
Finally, I summed up the viewpoint of the government and its plans for agriculture in general across Canada in these words:
The immediate and long term approach to the basic problem facing Canadian farmers is a recognition of the fact that the prosperity of Canada is indivisible and that a reasonably high and stable level of income in Canadian agriculture adds to the welfare of all Canadians.
That in general represented an enunciation of certain general principles and specific courses of legislation anticipated at that time. I now sum up once more the objectives of the government's agricultural policy.
We believe that agriculture is one of the most important sectors of the Canadian economy; that the prosperity of agriculture is an integral part of Canadian prosperity; that governments do have a responsibility in a constructive and effective manner to strengthen Canadian agriculture for in doing so the economy as a whole is strengthened. We believe that the national interest can best be served if we endeavour to do our utmost to develop efficiently and economically our resources, including agriculture; that farmers should have continuing opportunities to earn sufficient income to enjoy the benefits of our rapidly growing economy and the rising standards of living enjoyed by the population as a whole; and that a reasonably high and stable level of farm income is an essential prerequisite to a high level of employment and income in Canada generally.
We take the stand, and have, that government action to help Canadian agriculture to help itself is in the Canadian tradition of self-reliance and that government action primarily designed to provide and round out opportunities for farmers to do well on their own is a desirable objective.
Some of the agricultural problems are national in scope while others are regional. The policies that we have followed have been designed to deal with problems where they occur. Where the problems are national, national solutions are sought. Where the problems are regional and special, affecting, for instance the prairie wheat farmers, then solutions are designed to deal specifically with them. When policies are formulated to deal with the symptoms only, they do not solve the problems, but are likely to prolong their existence. All such policies usually do is to offer some temporary relief at the expense of somebody else.
We have endeavoured to place before the house a well thought out, carefully formulated and generally acceptable agricultural program as an integral part of the Canadian national development program. That being the general objective, I now want to refer to some of the stands that we have taken in that connection.

When we assumed office one of the first things we did was to examine the agricultural policies that had existed for a number of years under the former government. During many of those years the Progressive Conservative party insisted there was a need of basic reform measures in agriculture. We maintain that the very cornerstone of national development is a dynamic and flexible national agricultural policy.
Following that viewpoint we introduced, pursuant to the national agricultural policy of the government a long range farm policy comprehensive and co-ordinated. We did not in doing so neglect regional interests. We recognized in the most fundamental terms the national requirement that men and women on the land be given their right to a fair share of the national income.
In that connection I will merely summarize some of the legislative enactments which we have placed before parliament since then. There was the Farm Credit Act of 1959, authorizing long term mortgage credits to farmers and providing new hope for agriculture, particularly in the field of credit where it was so long desired and for which there was a clear and definite demand. Since the Farm Credit Act came into effect, some 1,900 loans have been extended involving some $16 million.
In addition, there was the Farm Improvement Loans Act available to farmers. Under the extension of this act in 1959 for a further three years, banks are guaranteed against losses up to 10 per cent of the aggregate principal amount lent by each bank, subject to an over-all government liability of $300 million in the three-year period.
Another subject of legislation is the Prairie Grain Advance Payment Act. This act authorizes the Canadian wheat board to make a payment to the producer in respect of a crop year as an advance on the initial payment for threshed grain in storage, but not in an elevator, prior to delivery to the board.
Then there was the legislation recently enacted, the Prairie Grain Provisional Payments Act, designed to help relieve the financial difficulties of grain producers in western Canada who, because of abnormal and unseasonal rain and snowstorms, had been prevented from harvesting their crops.
Then, as I mentioned a moment ago, the Crop Insurance Act of 1959 was passed to assist the provinces in establishing crop insurance legislation, and under which the federal government is authorized to make a grant in the amount of 50 per cent of any administrative cost, paying as well 20 per cent of any premiums arranged by the provinces. In addition to this, there was action

taken, as I mentioned earlier, under the Colombo plan designed to accelerate the exports of wheat and flour, either in the form of gifts or long term loans.
The Canadian gifts of wheat and flour were stepped up from $826,000 in 1955-56 to $2.7 million in 1956-57 and $19.5 million in 195859. In the current year, 1959-60, $11.2 million worth of wheat and flour has already been shipped in the form of gifts. In addition to this, the government has extended long term loans for the purchase of wheat and flour amounting to $24.2 million in 195758; $10.8 million in 1958-59.
Another source of action was the export credits insurance that extends a three-year credit for the sale of wheat and barley under the Export Credits Insurance Act. This has been in effect since 1952-53. Sales during the past two years under this act have averaged $17.5 million per year. These are but a few examples of what has been done, initially by legislation or by the extension of legislation already in effect, in order to bring about an extension in agricultural exports and in the development of a sound, practical agriculture.
Mention was made by the Minister of Agriculture a few moments ago of the South Saskatchewan dam and irrigation project. This was something that through the years had been bandied back and forth. This government acted immediately it was possible to do so, and has made the expectation of the completion of the dam a reality through a tremendous amount of financial assistance. The design and purpose of this is to make possible an improved agricultural prosperity in the area adjacent to the South Saskatchewan river which, for many years, has been an area in which drought has been a regular occurrence.
When in 1958 I placed before the house the facts as they were, as we saw them, and undertook to have brought before the house for its consideration an acreage payment of $1 per acre up to 200 acres the reception which that action received will be remembered by most hon. members in this house. Acreage payments were equated to the amounts or at least bore a relationship to the amounts that would be available to the farmer, and on which the highest domestic price was being paid to him rather than the selling price of wheat for export.
You will remember, sir, the reaction at that time. I am not going into it in detail, but to sum it up it was simply this: The payment of some $40 million to $41 million, as it turned out, was ridiculed by both the Liberals and C.C.F. parties and also condemned by various western farmer organizations. To
Supply-Agriculture
some the plan was looked upon with downright derision, although it represented a major benefit to the small farmers of western Canada. Today, as my correspondence indicates, many individual farmers in western Canada would have been most appreciative if something in the nature of that system could have been continued.
All hon. members will recall the reaction and the reception given to it in this house. In reality, it provided for farmers receiving an amount which as I said a moment ago, was roughly the number of bushels sold for domestic consumption in Canada. There are administrative difficulties in connection with the two-price system. In addition to that, there is the recognized fact that the two-price system, if it were carried into effect on the basis of the production of an individual farmer, would discriminate against small farmers, but would hurt most those who decided to feed their grain, or those who had a poor crop or nothing at all. Having given the fullest consideration to the two-price system, we determined that the plan used before was a fair and practical one.
There are some who advocate, and only recently representations were made in that connection by one of the farm organizations, that the two-price system should be brought into effect and the consumer must pay the higher price for bread. I have the record here of representations that were made in that connection in a submission of the western farm delegation liaison committee on January 30. On page 5, it says:
As an example, if the domestic price of wheat were increased by $1 per bushel, it would increase the price of a loaf of bread by less than two cents per loaf and would increase the revenue to the producer by about $55 million.
So far as the opposition is concerned, the stand taken by the opposition and represented by the Leader of the Opposition in this connection is most clear and definite. Speaking at Regina, according to a report in the Regina Leader-Post, in an article by Robert Moon, the Liberal leader told prairie farm delegates the most important thing the government could do is to preserve farm income stability. The Liberal leader did not want the farmer to be assisted by means of raising the price of food for the consumer. This was one of the representations that was brought before us, that the two-price system should be brought into effect and that the people of Canada as a whole could, by the simple expedient of that additional amount per loaf, provide the two-price system.
I pointed out the figures in connection with the two-price system, and I have pointed out one or two of them now. It was because of that that we, as I said earlier, followed

Sup p ly-A griculture
the course in 1958 of acreage payments. I should like now to refer to the reception that was given to that policy. On August 28, 1958 the hon. member for Assiniboia directed to me a question in which he said this, and I am just reading the pertinent parts unless someone wants me to read it all:
I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister arising out of a disturbing report in the Globe and Mail that the government will not make deficiency payments on western grain but will instead pay $1 per acre up to $200 per farmer, a most disturbing and inadequate amount.
The answer was as follows:
I am not going to announce government policy by way of comment on any newspaper article, but I can say this to the hon. gentleman. No matter what is done he will always say it is not enough.
To that answer he replied:
Especially if it is peanuts, like this announcement.
Mr. Chairman, $40 million from the people of Canada which went to the benefit of the western farmer, and particularly benefited the small farmer, would not, I am sure, today be so regarded, in the light of the retrospect of the last year and a half. Then the Leader of the Opposition said this, and I quote his words, as reported at page 4348 of Hansard of August 30, 1958:
We are quite sure, on this side, that the grain producers... will welcome this particular assistance, will welcome this particular grant, though they may be disappointed in the amount. I have no doubt that when my hon. friend from Assiniboia gets up immediately after I conclude he will call it peanuts.

I did that a couple of days ago. I shall call it a pittance today.
Then the Leader of the Opposition is reported as having said this:
Perhaps he may even refer to it as salted peanuts.
I read these remarks in the light of the attitude of western farmers today as they look back on the benefits that were theirs in consequence of that $1 per acre up to 200 acres. This brought great benefits to small farmers particularly.
There was a like attitude on the part of various farm leaders, one of whom referred to it as a pittance. I refer to James Patterson, president of the interprovincial farm union council, who also stated:
It takes a long time to pay bills with nickels.
Then again, the hon. member for Assiniboia stated in effect, that the present payment represented less than 10 per cent of the total amount of deficiency payments to farmers that they have asked for these two years. That is a summary of his words.
That was the reception that was given not by the average western farmer but by some who set themselves up to speak for the
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
western farmer. Then came the question of the request for deficiency payment. A moment ago I mentioned that the hon, member for Assiniboia stated that the $40 million represented about 10 per cent of the amount of the deficiency payment which the farmers expected to get for two years. What is now being asked is a deficiency payment, as I mentioned a moment ago, for the crop years 1955-56, 1956-57 and 1957-58, a total amount, if given, of well over $325 million, if not more.
All of us would like to be able to provide hundreds of millions of dollars, but I ask you, Mr. Chairman, what the situation would be if parliament were to vote such an amount in respect of the wheat, oats and barley produced during those years.
We believe that agriculture deserves every support. We have followed that course. We have examined the proposals for deficiency payments and we have spent many hours in the fullest examination of the matter. We did this because a large delegation came here almost a year ago representing all parts of the west. I for one, as a westerner, complimented them then, as I do now, for the manner in which they presented their case and for the degree of restraint they showed in the discussions that took place. We studied this problem.
In August, 1958 I set out the reasons why, in our opinion, deficiency payments were not the answer to the western farm situation. I am not going to repeat those reasons. They can be found at page 4306 of Hansard of that date.
These proposals, as we consider, after giving the matter the fullest and most comprehensive study, tend to neglect the needs of the smaller farmers. They provide no aid to the farmer who has suffered a crop failure. They give little to the mixed farmer and livestock raiser who markets a limited amount of wheat.
However attractive it is to secure that amount of money to be distributed among the western farmers whose needs I know, and whose requests I view with more than usual sympathy, the proposals had weaknesses. The most grave weakness is that the payment of deficiency payments would not touch the fundamental problems of the farmer on the land.
The most outstanding characteristic of the prairie farm economy is the variability of income. In 1937 the crop in most parts of the west was scarcely worth harvesting. Three years later and again in 1942 very large crops were threshed.

As I said a moment ago, one of the major reasons for the South Saskatchewan river dam was the fact that such failures in certain areas were typical of farming in those areas.
Technological improvements, and marketing techniques, have both tended to reduce some of this income variability but he would be irresponsible who would suggest that any easy solution will be found to the age old problem of farm income variability.
The farmer who suffers most acutely from this problem of income variability is the small farmer. Also affected is the farmer in a district that has a poor crop record as a result of natural hazards. These so-called deficiency payments are not deficiency payments at all in the term used in the Agricultural Stabilization Act or in the support programs in various other countries.
Under the stabilization act a deficiency payment is the amount paid to a farmer to bring his return up to the price guaranteed him for the current year. It therefore involves the concept of forward pricing. The payments requested on western wheat, oats and barley are retroactive flat payments rather than forward prices. What they, in fact, amount to is a request to put into effect in Canada the same kind of fixed support prices which have been in effect in the United States and which have resulted in the piling up of such large surpluses of wheat and other commodities in that country.
The proposal is that the price of wheat, oats and barley should be the same for those years as it was, on the average, in the eight-year period from 1945-46 to 1952-53 when grain was at the highest price in our history. This, in effect, would be the same as the United States fixed formula. It differs from that only in that a different period of years has been taken as the base period, and the relationship of the price asked for to the cost of goods and services bought by farmers has been left out.
Mr. Chairman, one thing concerns me about the time and I do not want in any way to place the Leader of the Opposition or other hon. members in the position of not being able to reply today. If I am not out of order, I would like to suggest, with unanimous consent of the house, that the private members' hour from five to six o'clock might, to the extent necessary, be given up. I make that suggestion because I do not want anyone to say that I came in late in the afternoon so as to make it impossible for hon. members to have their say.

I am sure that would be agreeable to us.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Then I do not want to leave the Leader of the Opposition in an impossible position, and I will have to conclude after a few preliminary remarks and proceed later, I presume next week, to place before the country the views of the government on this question.
I mentioned a moment ago that there would be no benefit to any extent to the small farmer. An examination of the record in that connection shows that 9.4 per cent of the holders of wheat board permits have 99 or less specified acres; nine and four tenths per cent of the grain producers would, under this proposal, receive 2 per cent of the aid that would be extended under the deficiency payment. Some 25.5 per cent of the holders of wheat board permits have between 100 and 199 specified acres, and to them would go some 12 per cent of the total of the payments. In other words, 35 per cent of the smaller farmers on the prairies would receive only 14 per cent of the proposed deficiency payment if this scheme were brought into effect, and the remaining 86 per cent of the payment would go to 65 per cent of the farmers.
The proposed program would give a maximum of $1,500 a year to each farmer, or $4,500 to the largest farmers in a district. But to the small neighbours, or the farmer in an adjoining district who had suffered a series of crop failures, little or nothing would be paid. In other words, if this plan were carried into effect the greatest help would go to the people who need it the least.
The other fundamental weakness in the program is that it could not fail to intensify the grain surplus problem. If the proposal were a deficiency payment in the sense in which that term is ordinarily used, this might not be the case. In the stabilization act a deficiency payment is an amount paid to bring a return up to a guaranteed level for the current year. This means that the commodity in question tends to find its

Supply-Agriculture
own level in the market place, and the tendency is for the surplus to be cleared away by the purchases of consumers. The hard fact is that the deficiency payment total is indistinguishable from the inflexible price supports which have been in effect in the United States which, as I have said, have accumulated unmanageable surpluses in that jountry.
I have already referred to the cost, but it is more than just the cost of the payment to the western farmers. It would also involve an extra cost for storage. The government last year paid $39,800,000 for storing grain in excess of 178 million bushels for which it was not responsible. There would also be the additional cost of moving the grain to consumers in a situation of world surplus.
As to oats and barley, it is probable that the United States would exclude these coarse grains from their markets or would place countervailing duties against them.
In summary, it has been urged that this government introduce a program of costly deficiency payments which will do relatively little for at least 35 per cent of the smaller grain farmers it is designed to help. It would increase surpluses and, in respect to oats and barley, would shrink markets. We recognize the principle that public money should be used to relieve distress on the basis of need, and any scheme which gives no help, or very little, to those who are most in need is socially indefensible. Any proposal to augment the admitted income deficiency of western grain producers must be of such a nature that the bulk of the assistance provided is directed to those most in need of it.
We recognize that certain grain farmers in western Canada require assistance, but we are unable to accept the suggested program of deficiency payments for the reasons which I have outlined. We must again conclude, as we did in 1958, that the fixed support type of deficiency payment is not the most equitable way of giving assistance to western farmers during this period of adjustment while the national farm program begins to take hold and work for the farmer.
In saying that I want to make this very clear. I was surprised at the reaction in 1958 when we placed before the house a plan whereby payments were made on an acreage basis. The opposition spoke strongly against it. In the province of Saskatchewan the members of the C.C.F. ridiculed it, condemned it, and held it up to public scorn. I felt at that time, and I feel now, that it represented a step which would have given the farmers new hope, and that it represented the only 
way in which farmers could be helped, particularly small farmers, and enabled to carry on.
In regard to the other matters upon which I intend to speak, I will reserve that opportunity until later in order to give the Leader of the Opposition the right and the privilege of placing his views generally before the house.
I will conclude by saying this: there are many other matters in connection with agricultural policy to which I shall direct attention. We shall always be ready to consider appropriate measures to benefit agriculture, but I say through you, Mr. Chairman, to the western farmers that when we took the course we did in 1958 to help the small farmers, the opposition we received from the opposition in general and from the members of the C.C.F. party in particular did come as a surprise. It came as a surprise that such an attitude should be taken. I conclude by saying that with reference to the other matters to which I had intended to direct my attention, I will do so at the very first opportunity which comes to me during discussion of the estimates of the Department of Agriculture.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The Prime Minister having spoken for 40 minutes, and the Minister of Agriculture for 15 minutes before him, and the C.C.F. party not being willing to give up 15 or 20 minutes of the private members' hour, I find that I have six minutes in which to put the position of this party, generally, before the committee and this country. That does not give me much time, but I can say that after more than a year of consideration of certain requests made by farm organizations with regard to deficiency payments on grain or other methods of maintaining farm stability the Prime Minister has made a statement in reply to those representations which have been repeated, and that statement, stripped of its verbiage, while not agreeing to the proposals made by the farm organizations, means that the Prime Minister and the government have no definite proposals to put before parliament at this time with regard to the emergency and the proposals raised by the farm organizations.
During this year the position of agriculture in this country has deteriorated, and the cost-price squeeze felt by farmers is worse than it was a year ago, and the farmers' share of the national income is less than it was a year ago. The Minister of Finance has stated that the national income may increase during this year by 7 per cent, but at the same time we learned today that net agricultural income in 1959 has declined by 7 per cent. Therefore, if any

of those terms were justified a year ago, they certainly are justified today in the light of the deterioration of the farm situation.
In regard to the request by the farm organizations for deficiency payments on grain, speaking for my party, I said on May 27, 1959:
It was recognized by the Liberal party that the balance in the national economy had in recent years turned against certain agricultural and other primary producers. That balance should be restored.
The position is even worse now than it was in those days. I went on to say:
It was recognized that difficulties by grain growers were, in recent years, due particularly to farm costs increasing and declining incomes.
Then I continued:
So far as the Liberal party was concerned, they were on record as supporting the principle of deficiency payments when appropriate.
Declining incomes and increasing costs seem to us to make the situation now appropriate for this kind of assistance to the farmers and grain producers of this country. We feel that grain is a suitable commodity for this particular method of maintaining and stabilizing farm income. The price mechanism and marketing procedure in respect to grain are very different from those existing in the case of hogs and eggs which are not, we think, susceptible to this kind of assistance. The Prime Minister's argument against deficiency payments states that one of the reasons why deficiency prices should not be put into effect is that they will create surpluses.
In any event, we feel in view of the situation which is now confronting the grain producers of this country that deficiency payments would be an appropriate method of helping the producers. It is a method based on principles which can be applied generally, and therefore can be supported at this time. When we have an opportunity we shall put forward in greater detail proposals based on this principle. We support deficiency payments in accordance with a formula which would take into account rising costs. In other words, the deficiency payment would be based on the increased cost of production of the farmer compared with a base period when costs were relatively stable.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: What base period?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The Prime Minister cannot ask me questions now, because I have one minute in which to complete this statement. If I had more time, I would be glad to answer him.
That is our position. We favour a system of deficiency payments for grain producers which would take into account rising costs. This would be no handout. It would be no
Private Bills
ad hoc solution. It would be compensation based on a formula which I shall be glad at an appropriate time to discuss in detail. We think that in view of what has happened in the last year, in view of the situation in agriculture, a 7 per cent reduction in net agricultural income against a gross national income which is increasing, we are told, by 6 per cent; in view of the increase in the severity of the cost-price squeeze the time has come when the grain producer is entitled to this kind of assistance based on principles-an assistance which will not be considered as a handout.
Therefore, we share in the disappointment which will be felt by all farmers in this country at the entirely negative statement made by the Prime Minister. All the Prime Minister has done in this statement is to tell us how much this government has done for the farmer in the past two years while the net agricultural income has gone down 7 per cent. The time has come when the farmer is entitled to a better deal than that, and at the proper time, if we get the opportunity, we shall put that deal forward in all its aspects.

Q. What is your full name?
A. George Roland Foucher.
Q. What is your age?
A. Forty-three.
Q. Where do you live?
A. Montreal.
Q. What is your occupation?
A. Insurance investigator.
I should like to ask the sponsor of this bill what special qualifications does an insurance investigator have for this particular business? It appears to me that in this particular instance it is a false label that the gentleman is using. Certainly in this instance he would not be doing any insurance investigating. Has he any qualifications that make him any more capable of doing investigations into divorce than anyone else because of the fact that he lists himself as an insurance investigator?

Mr. Chairman, I suppose the obvious and short answer is that an insurance investigator spends most of his

time studying collisions between two automobiles, and therefore it takes only a step further to study collisions between two human beings who wind up in divorce actions. The long answer is that this is the gentleman to whom I referred on Tuesday when the same matters were brought forth. It is true that he does come before parliament in, say, half a dozen or a dozen cases to give evidence. He has chosen to classify himself as an insurance investigator. I presume by that means he is trying to cover himself with more respectability than the other people who simply come and say that they are private investigators.
The man in question, as I mentioned last time, was the subject of some concern between myself and the chairman of the committee in the other place. We felt that it would be better if he took out a private licence so that if there were any hints of malpractice-and I must say immediately in defence of this gentleman whose name was mentioned, Mr. Foucher, that I have never heard of any at all

we felt it would be better if he intended to make a career of this, and intended to take part in at least half a dozen or a dozen investigations a year, for him to be properly licensed so that he would find himself under whatever advantages there are from being licensed in the province of Quebec, and would also be subject to any penalties the province might choose to inflict on an errant private investigator.
Again, so far as this gentleman is concerned, I have read his evidence in this case with great care, and it is very much like his evidence in other oases. He is very thorough-going in his methods. It seems to me that if he did become a private detective or received that licence he might very well become president of the Montreal private detective agency or association because he is an extremely thorough and capable investigator.

A. Yes, I did.
It would appear to me that a man who was so well versed as Mr. Foucher appears to be in investigations used some very unethical methods in obtaining evidence because would it not have been just as simple for him to have copied the name on the doorplate instead of stealing it?
From reading the evidence I am in agreement with the sponsor of the bill that Mr. Foucher, who is 43 years old, is probably not in the worst class of these investigators. His evidence is straightforward. I have seen these gentlemen give evidence before the house committee but when they give evidence before the Senate committee do they read their evidence? Is the evidence all written down? How are these private investigators able to be as factual as they are in a particular instance? I would presume that over a period of time the investigator has acted in a number of these cases and it is always surprising to me that he is so sure about exactly what happened when he is carrying on 10 or 12 investigations in various parts of the city over the same period.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on the same point of order, the hon. member for Timiska-ming has given you his opinion. Has he any authority for the statements he is making or for the suggestion that he can go into this evidence, examine it and enlarge upon it?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: What authority have you?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I have the authority that there is no such authority, and unless you produce authority it cannot be done.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
On the point of order raised by the Minister of Public Works, I would like to go back to standing order 59 (2) which is as follows:
Speeches in committee of the whole house must be strictly relevant to the item or clause under consideration.
Therefore, the only thing we can discuss in these divorce bills is what is enumerated in the preamble to the bill. This committee, of course, has nothing to do with the question of whether the committee went outside the preamble. That we cannot discuss. So we must keep our discussion absolutely relevant to what is in the preamble of the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, can you read into the record the preamble of the particular bill we are discussing so that the hon. member, if he can read, will see it?

speechtext: I am reading it, you are not.

speechtext:

Whereas . .. residing at... in the province of Quebec ... wife of . .. who is domiciled in Canada and residing at the said city, has by her petition alleged that they were married on ... on the ... at the said city, she then being . . . and whereas by 79951-0-112J

speechtext: Thank you Mr. Chairman. That is the point. All we have to do is either to approve the bill or disapprove it. But we cannot go behind the bill. The finding has been made that adultery has been committed. We are not a court of appeal, and with great respect I would ask you, Mr. Chairman, to stay within the purport of your own finding, and that is that we cannot go beyond the preamble of the bill and cannot go behind the adultery which has been proved. Nor can we adduce further and irrelevant evidence.

Mr. Chairman, on the point of order, on this question of private bills I have never heard it suggested in the committee before that it was not competent for the committee of the whole with a private bill based on an allegation of fact, to examine into that fact and the evidence adduced in a standing committee of the house, in this case the miscellaneous private bills committee. It is quite common to question that evidence in detail and go over it and argue it and suggest that the standing committee making the report was wrong, or misinterpreted the evidence, and so on. I have never heard that suggestion before and I must say, with deference to my hon. colleague the Minister of Public Works, my classmate, that his position is not tenable. However regrettable it may be, we do have to listen to some of this unpleasant evidence.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: As long as the evidence is relevant to the debate.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the suggestion has been made that this was a fairly straightforward case. I would agree that it reads that way except for one or two matters. One is that we have two investigators doing the investigating and making the statements, and I consider their information to be always suspect, having found some of it not to be reliable. I think one of our problems in granting this divorce is whether we would be better advised to try to obtain a reconciliation between the two people, or whether we should grant this particular bill for their relief.
The husband has not been irresponsible. The fact that he bought five cars does not necessarily make him irresponsible. That would all depend, I think, on how much money he was making at the time. The gentleman named is employed as a fireman in

the Verdun fire department. I would assume that because he is in the service of the municipality he has, probably, a much better reputation than this particular document would indicate. The fact that he has been employed there for a number of years would indicate to me-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. The hon. member is discussing the private life of one of the parties concerned and I must ask him to come back to the bill.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
What I am suggesting is that collusion may have been a factor in this particular case, and I am suggesting that though the evidence goes in one direction, the characters of the people involved do not indicate that this is what one would necessarily expect. One of the people involved was a nurse, and the other was a fireman, and I am suggesting that because these investigators have been called in there may have been some consideration between the man and his wife as to obtaining this divorce, and if there was any question about that I am quite sure the committee would not want to grant a divorce when they are assuming that the grounds for adultery have already been proved in this case.
I point out that one of these two people was a nurse, and the other a fireman. They are stable factors in the community, and it is not likely that they would do what has been alleged in this particular case. This is a fairly comprehensive and straightforward case and I should like to read the questioning by Mr. Cohen:
Q. Mr. Wiseman, I show you a photograph, can you identify this exhibit No. 2?

I saw him enter the office, came out shortly thereafter, and he took a cabin which is located just about two doors away from the office, unit No. 6, I believe it was.
Q. Was he with the petitioner on that occasion?
A. Definitely not.
Q. Could you describe the respondent, and the co-respondent?
A. The respondent is a heavy set man about 200 lbs. in his middle or late 30's, has a mustache, light brown hair. The co-respondent is a woman about 24 or 25 years old, blond, very fair, about 5 ft. 4 or 5 inches tall.
Q. Was there any conversation when you went into that cabin?
A. Yes. What happened was, when I had seen him enter the cabin I parked my car in a nonconspicuous spot, and I surveyed the area and the cabin. At about 10 p.m. the lights in the cabin went off. I waited some one-half hour or so, then called our office and asked that my associate, Mr. Hiddell, join me down there at the motel. Mr. Riddell probably arrived about 11.15, or there abouts.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: topic
Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I wonder if I may have permission to say a word about the request which was made by the leader of the house a moment ago that the house should give leave to proceed today with the second and third readings of the appropriation bill? Hon. members will recall that the various stages were passed earlier today, but when you asked about second reading the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) said: "Later this day." The leader of the house has raised the question now

as to whether consent might not be given to proceed with the later stages of the appropriation measure today. I understand that the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith), speaking for the official opposition, has declined to give that unanimous consent. May I put this point to him and to the house: it bad been indicated earlier in the week that it would be the intention of the government on Monday next to offer a supply motion. Standing order 56 provides that on such an occasion such a motion must be the first motion of business. It also provides in subsection 2 that on Tuesday, the second day of such debate, the resumption of such debate must be the first order of business. That would mean that apart from unanimous consent of the house we would not be in a position to return to this appropriation measure before Wednesday. Mr. Speaker, I am asking hon. members if they will give unanimous consent to our proceeding now or, at any rate, to waive that provision on Monday so that we can take this appropriation measure as the first order of business on Monday.
There are some very urgent matters provided for in these times, and I have to tell the house that if this measure is not passed right away in time to be in the Senate on Tuesday we shall be obliged to stop making certain payments, because we simply have not the money for the purpose. Some payments are not proceeding that are urgently desired now. I make this plea to the house. If the house is not prepared to give unanimous consent to proceeding now I would urge that the house do give unanimous consent to our proceeding as the first order of business on Monday with this measure and put it through its remaining stages, notwithstanding the provisions of standing order 56.

Mr. Speaker, I regret I did not see the leader of the house come into the chamber during the committee stage at five minutes to six o'clock. I had been watching for him. I appreciate the difficulties in which the government finds itself on this, but perhaps I will not say anything about some of the things that went on earlier today that maybe took more time than was expected on this matter in the committee stage, but I am unable to give the consent at the moment.
As I understand the matter, the other place meets on Tuesday night. I think I am correct on that, and I would be very glad to take up the question of having consent given at some appropriate time in order to have the measure before the other place without delay, when they meet again, so that there would be no time lost by reason of my withholding
Business of the House
consent at the moment. I shall be very glad to do that. I think that will meet the difficulties in which the Minister of Finance finds himself at the moment.

Mr. Speaker, this group, realizing the circumstances and the explanation of the Minister of Finance, is quite willing to support a waiver of the rules for unanimous consent on Monday in order that this measure be passed and receive royal assent on Tuesday.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the house prepared to make an order now? Is the hon. member for Ottawa West prepared to agree that an order of the house be made now that, notwithstanding rule 56, the measure which has had first reading be taken up on Monday?

I would prefer to speak to the leader of the government in the house and give formal consent on Monday, rather than give it now, so that we can fix a mutually convenient time. It is a very simple thing. As I understand it, so long as it is done on Monday there will be no loss of time involved in the ultimate passage of the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Unless I know now I would, in suggesting the business for Monday, have to call for private members' day on Monday so that government business would proceed on Tuesday, on which occasion this would be the first matter for consideration; whereas I have indicated already we intend having a supply motion on Monday and Tuesday.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Let me put it this way. The house will take up this bill again no later than the first order of business on Tuesday.
That is agreeable.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: If agreement is not obtained on Monday, then at least the bill will be taken as the first order of business on Tuesday.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if it could
be the first order of business on Monday I am sure everybody would be satisfied. I do not want to be placed in the position now of having to change the order of business for next week.
I expect it can be the first business on Monday, but I have not the assurance of one person who desires to speak that he will be available for the opening of the house on Monday.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I appeal to hon. members to have this matter clarified because it is so important and so urgent; and there

Business of the House are such important payments that will simply not be made; payments that have been made hitherto but can no longer be made unless we pass this measure through. I do not think the matter should be left in the air; I do not think the government can take the responsibility of leaving the matter up in the air. In appealing to the hon. gentleman I remind him that in my 15 years in the house I never remember a case where objection has been taken to proceeding with all stages of an appropriation measure on the same day once the resolutions have been reported out of committee of supply.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to pursue this situation further. I have made it perfectly clear that there will be no delay whatever in the passage of this bill, and I have indicated that it was purely a matter of arranging the time on Monday for the discussion of this particular bill. I hope it will be possible to have it the first thing on Monday but I should like to avoid giving that firm commitment at this moment.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I will be satisfied if an order of the house issues now that this bill be taken up and considered on Monday.
That is all right.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The house understands the point; the business on Monday is a supply motion, but notwithstanding that the house now orders that this bill be appointed for consideration on Monday. If not by agreement, it is definitely understood that it will be called in the course of Monday.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: And the understanding is that all stages will be considered.
Yes, that is right.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: And that all stages will be considered on Monday? Agreed?
Agreed.
Is the minister in a position to indicate the business for Wednesday, following the supply motion?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker: I will have to announce that on Monday night.
It being nine minutes past six o'clock, the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
